course.title: Music Theory Fundamentals
course.description: A ground-up tour of how written music works — pitch and the staff, rhythm and meter, scales, intervals, and the chords built from them. Assembled from openly-licensed OER Commons music theory material (CC BY).

questions.prompt: A musical staff is made of…
questions.explanation: The staff is five lines with four spaces between them — see 'Pitch and the staff'.

questions.prompt: The treble clef is also called the…
questions.explanation: The treble clef curls around the line for G4, so it is the G clef — see 'Pitch and the staff'.

questions.prompt: In 4/4 time, a half note lasts…
questions.explanation: A half note is half of a whole note (4 beats), so it lasts 2 beats — see 'Rhythm and meter'.

questions.prompt: The C major scale contains how many sharps or flats?
questions.explanation: C major is all white keys: C D E F G A B — see 'Scales and key signatures'.

questions.prompt: The step pattern of a major scale is…
options: W H W W H W W
W W H W W W H
H W H W H W H
W W W H H W W
questions.explanation: Major = whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half — see 'Scales and key signatures'.

questions.prompt: The interval from C up to G is a…
questions.explanation: C up to G spans five letter names and seven semitones — a perfect fifth. See 'Intervals'.

questions.prompt: A major triad is built from a root plus…
options: a minor third and a perfect fifth
a major third and a perfect fifth
a major third and a minor seventh
questions.explanation: A major triad stacks a major third and a perfect fifth above the root — see 'Triads and basic harmony'.

questions.prompt: The relative minor of C major is…
questions.explanation: A minor shares C major's key signature (no sharps or flats) — see 'Scales and key signatures'.

lessons.title: Pitch and the staff: reading notes
lessons.grammar_note: Musical alphabet: A B C D E F G, then it starts over.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the lines and spaces of the treble and bass staff and locate middle C. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, how many lines make up a staff, and how many spaces sit between them?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds. We write pitches on a *staff* of five lines and four spaces. Notes are named with the first seven letters — A B C D E F G — and then the alphabet repeats; the distance from one letter to its next repeat (say C to the next C) is an *octave*. A *clef* fixes which letters go where. The *treble clef* (G clef) sets its lines, bottom to top, as E G B D F ('Every Good Boy Does Fine') and its spaces as F A C E ('FACE'). The *bass clef* (F clef) sets its lines as G B D F A and its spaces as A C E G. *Middle C* (C4) sits on one short *ledger line* just below the treble staff, or just above the bass staff.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Read up the treble staff from middle C: C4 sits on a ledger line below the staff; the note just above it, D4, hangs below the bottom line; E4 sits on the bottom line; F4 in the first space; G4 on the second line; A4 in the second space; B4 on the middle line. So a note on the middle line of the treble staff is B4, and the space just above it is C5.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) What note is in the top space of the treble staff? (2) What note is on the top line of the treble staff? (3) On the bass staff, what note sits on the middle (third) line? (4) True or false: the treble spaces spell FACE from bottom to top. (5) Middle C is written on a ledger line — above or below the treble staff? Answers: (1) E5, (2) F5, (3) D3, (4) true, (5) below.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading the treble line mnemonic top-to-bottom — it runs bottom-to-top (E G B D F). Mistake: thinking after G comes H — it wraps back to A. Exit: (a) Name the treble lines bottom to top. (b) After the note G, what letter comes next? Answers: E G B D F; A.

lessons.title: Rhythm and meter
lessons.grammar_note: Time signature: top number = beats per measure, bottom number = which note value gets one beat.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compare note values and read a simple time signature. Warm-up: in 4/4 time, how many beats does a half note last?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Rhythm is how long notes last. Each note value is worth half the one before it: a *whole note* = 4 beats, a *half note* = 2, a *quarter note* = 1, an *eighth note* = ½, a *sixteenth note* = ¼ (counting a quarter note as one beat). A *dot* after a note adds half of that note's value again, so a *dotted half note* lasts 3 beats (2 + 1). Music is grouped into *measures* by bar lines, and a *time signature* tells you how each measure is counted: the top number is how many beats per measure, and the bottom number says which note value counts as one beat (4 = quarter note, 8 = eighth note). So 4/4 means four quarter-note beats per measure, 3/4 is a three-beat waltz, and 6/8 groups six eighth notes.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Fill one 4/4 measure (4 beats) exactly. One whole note fills it (4). So does two half notes (2 + 2). So does a half note plus two quarters (2 + 1 + 1). So does a dotted half note plus a quarter (3 + 1). And four quarter notes (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) fill it too — every combination must sum to 4.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: In 4/4, give the beat count for each: (1) a quarter note, (2) a dotted half note, (3) two eighth notes together, (4) a whole note, (5) a half note plus a quarter note. Answers: (1) 1 beat, (2) 3 beats, (3) 1 beat total, (4) 4 beats, (5) 3 beats.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the bottom number of a time signature counts beats — it names the note value that gets the beat. Mistake: reading a dot as doubling the note (it adds only half). Exit: (a) In 3/4, how many beats per measure? (b) How long is a dotted quarter note in 4/4? Answers: three; 1½ beats.

lessons.title: Scales and key signatures
lessons.grammar_note: Major scale steps: W W H W W W H. Natural minor: W H W W H W W.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Build a major and a natural minor scale by note name and explain what a key signature does. Warm-up: how many sharps or flats does C major have?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *scale* is an ordered ladder of pitches within an octave. Between notes we count *whole steps* (W, two semitones) and *half steps* (H, one semitone). A *major scale* follows W W H W W W H. Starting on C that gives C D E F G A B C — all natural notes, no sharps or flats. A *natural minor scale* follows W H W W H W W; starting on A it gives A B C D E F G A, also all naturals. Because A minor uses the same notes as C major, it is C major's *relative minor* — every major key has a relative minor a minor third below its tonic that shares its *key signature* (the sharps or flats printed at the start of the staff). Sharps are added in the order F C G D A E B; flats in the reverse order, B E A D G C F.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Build D major with W W H W W W H starting on D: D →(W) E →(W) F# →(H) G →(W) A →(W) B →(W) C# →(H) D. The two altered notes are F# and C#, so D major's key signature has two sharps. Now build E natural minor with W H W W H W W: E →(W) F# →(H) G →(W) A →(W) B →(H) C →(W) D →(W) E. Its only altered note is F#, matching G major — so E minor is the relative minor of G major.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Spell the F major scale (hint: one flat). (2) How many sharps are in G major, and which note? (3) What is the relative minor of G major? (4) Name the first three sharps in order. (5) Is the step from E to F a whole step or a half step? Answers: (1) F G A B-flat C D E F, (2) one sharp, F#, (3) E minor, (4) F# C# G#, (5) a half step.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forcing every scale to use only natural notes — the W-W-H-W-W-W-H pattern forces sharps or flats in most keys. Mistake: reusing a letter name (e.g. spelling D major with G-flat instead of F#) — each of the seven letters appears once per scale. Exit: (a) How many sharps in D major? (b) Which minor key shares C major's key signature? Answers: two (F# and C#); A minor.

questions.prompt: The spaces of the treble staff, bottom to top, spell…
questions.explanation: F, A, C, E — the word 'FACE'.

questions.prompt: In 4/4 time, a dotted half note lasts…
questions.explanation: A half note (2) plus half its value again (1) equals 3 beats.

questions.prompt: The C major scale contains…
questions.explanation: C D E F G A B — all natural notes.

questions.prompt: The step pattern of the major scale is…
options: W H W W H W W
W W H W W W H
W W W H W W H
H W W H W W W
questions.explanation: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.

questions.prompt: The key signature of D major contains…
questions.explanation: Building D major raises F and C to F# and C#.

questions.prompt: The relative minor of C major is…
questions.explanation: A minor shares C major's notes and key signature.

lessons.title: Intervals
lessons.grammar_note: An interval = a number (count letter names, inclusive) + a quality (perfect, major, minor, and so on).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name an interval's size and quality from two note names. Warm-up: how many letter names lie from C up to G, counting both ends?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An *interval* is the distance between two pitches. It has a *number* — count the letter names inclusively, so C to E is a third (C, D, E) — and a *quality*. Fourths, fifths, unisons, and octaves come in *perfect* form; seconds, thirds, sixths, and sevenths come in *major* or *minor* form. Quality is pinned down by counting *semitones*: a major second = 2, minor third = 3, major third = 4, perfect fourth = 5, perfect fifth = 7, major sixth = 9, and a perfect octave = 12. Lowering a major interval by one semitone (without changing its letter names) makes it minor.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: C to E: the letters C-D-E make a third, and C to E is 4 semitones — a *major third*. C to E-flat: still the letters C-D-E, so still a third, but now 3 semitones — a *minor third*. C to G: the letters C-D-E-F-G make a fifth, and C to G is 7 semitones — a *perfect fifth*. C to F: a fourth (C-D-E-F), 5 semitones — a *perfect fourth*. E to G: a third (E-F-G), 3 semitones — a *minor third*.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Name each interval (size and quality): (1) D up to A, (2) C up to E, (3) A up to C, (4) C up to F, (5) G up to D, (6) E up to G-sharp. Answers: (1) perfect fifth, (2) major third, (3) minor third, (4) perfect fourth, (5) perfect fifth, (6) major third.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: counting the steps between notes instead of the letter names — the number is inclusive, so C to E is a third, not a second. Mistake: ignoring quality — C to E and C to E-flat are both thirds but sound different (major vs minor). Exit: (a) How many semitones in a perfect fifth? (b) Is C to E-flat major or minor? Answers: seven; minor.

lessons.title: Triads and basic harmony
lessons.grammar_note: A triad = root + third + fifth, stacked in thirds.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Build the four triad types by note name and identify the chords of a major key. Warm-up: a major triad stacks which two intervals above its root?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *triad* is a three-note chord built by stacking thirds: a *root*, a third above it, and a fifth above the root. The type depends on which thirds you stack. A *major triad* = major third + perfect fifth (C E G). A *minor triad* = minor third + perfect fifth (A C E). A *diminished triad* = minor third + diminished fifth (B D F). An *augmented triad* = major third + augmented fifth (C E G#). Build a triad on every note of a scale and you get that key's *diatonic* chords. In C major they are, with Roman numerals: I = C major (C E G), ii = D minor (D F A), iii = E minor (E G B), IV = F major (F A C), V = G major (G B D), vi = A minor (A C E), and vii° = B diminished (B D F). Chords move in *progressions*; two of the most common are I–IV–V–I and I–V–vi–IV.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Build the G major triad: root G, up a major third to B, up a perfect fifth from G to D → G B D. Build the E minor triad: root E, up a minor third to G, perfect fifth E to B → E G B. Build the D major triad: root D, major third to F#, fifth D to A → D F# A. Harmonize in C major: the V chord is built on G, giving G B D — a G major triad.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Spell the F major triad. (2) Spell the A minor triad. (3) Spell the D minor triad. (4) In C major, which triad is the IV chord, and spell it. (5) What quality is the triad B-D-F? Answers: (1) F A C, (2) A C E, (3) D F A, (4) F major, F A C, (5) diminished.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: building a triad by skipping the wrong notes — always stack thirds (every other letter): C-E-G, not C-D-G. Mistake: assuming every diatonic chord is major — in a major key the ii, iii, and vi chords are minor and the vii° is diminished. Exit: (a) Spell the C major triad. (b) In C major, is the ii chord (built on D) major or minor? Answers: C E G; minor.

items.translation: the five lines and four spaces on which notes are written
items.example: A note on the bottom line of the treble staff is E4.

items.translation: the distance from one pitch to the next note of the same letter name
items.example: From C4 up to C5 is one octave.

items.translation: two stacked numbers showing beats per measure (top) and which note gets the beat (bottom)
items.example: In 4/4 there are four quarter-note beats per measure.

items.translation: the sharps or flats printed at the start of the staff that set the key
items.example: One sharp (F#) in the key signature means G major or E minor.

items.translation: the distance between two pitches, named by a number and a quality
items.example: C up to G is a perfect fifth.

items.translation: a three-note chord of a root, a third, and a fifth stacked in thirds
items.example: The C major triad is C E G.

questions.prompt: The interval from C up to E is a…
questions.explanation: A third spanning 4 semitones is a major third.

questions.prompt: The interval from C up to G is a…
questions.explanation: Five letter names and 7 semitones — a perfect fifth.

questions.prompt: A major triad is a root plus…
options: a minor third and a perfect fifth
a major third and a perfect fifth
a major third and an augmented fifth
questions.explanation: Major third + perfect fifth, as in C E G.

questions.prompt: The triad C E G is…
questions.explanation: A major third (C–E) and perfect fifth (C–G) make it C major.

questions.prompt: In C major, the V chord is…
questions.explanation: Built on the fifth degree G: G B D, a G major triad.

questions.prompt: The triad B D F is…
questions.explanation: A minor third (B–D) and a diminished fifth (B–F) make it diminished.

lessons.title: Applied project: compose and harmonize a melody

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Compose an eight-bar melody in a major key and harmonize it with chords drawn from that key. You will write everything with note names and Roman numerals — no notation software required.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Choose a key (C major and G major are easiest) and state its notes and key signature. 2) Pick a time signature (4/4 or 3/4) and write eight measures of rhythm whose beats add up correctly in each measure. 3) Assign a scale note to each beat to form your melody, beginning and ending on the tonic (the key's first note). 4) Harmonize by choosing one diatonic triad per measure from I ii iii IV V vi vii°, and write out each chord's three note names. 5) End the last two bars with a V–I progression for a sense of closure.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Every measure's note values sum to the time signature. ✔ Every melody note and every chord belongs to your chosen key (no stray accidentals). ✔ Each chord is spelled correctly as a stack of thirds (e.g. G major = G B D). ✔ The melody starts and ends on the tonic and the final cadence is V–I. If all four hold, you have written a small, theoretically sound piece.
